text: An NVIDIA A100 is enormous — up to eighty gibibytes of memory and enough compute to train a large model from scratch. A lot of real workloads never come close to needing that much, especially inference, yet the default Kubernetes GPU model from last lesson hands out GPUs as whole units only. This lesson covers the two real mechanisms — time-slicing and MIG — that fix that waste.

Under the default model, a pod requesting one GPU claims the entire physical card, even if it only uses a tenth of its memory and compute. The other ninety percent sits idle, and you're still paying for all of it. Time-slicing and Multi-Instance GPU solve this differently, with genuinely different tradeoffs between simplicity and isolation.

Time-slicing lets the device plugin advertise more copies of nvidia.com/gpu than physical GPUs exist, configured through a ConfigMap — four replicas means four pods can land on the same card, with the GPU's own hardware scheduler context-switching between them. The tradeoff is real: no memory or fault isolation, so pods sharing a card can still trip each other's out-of-memory errors under heavy load.

MIG works at the hardware level instead, available on A100 and H100-class GPUs: it physically partitions one GPU into up to seven GPU instances, each with its own dedicated memory and compute slices, genuinely isolated from the others. Profiles like 1g.10gb describe the split directly — one compute slice, ten gibibytes of memory — and each partitioned instance becomes its own requestable Kubernetes resource.

Time-slicing works on any NVIDIA GPU and is simple to turn on, at the cost of isolation — a reasonable trade for small, forgiving workloads. MIG needs supporting hardware and a fixed partition layout chosen up front, but delivers real isolation for genuinely multi-tenant use. Either way, a large training job still wants a whole GPU to itself — sharing is an inference problem.

That's the full provisioning picture for this chapter: quota and Terraform, drivers and the container toolkit, the device plugin that makes GPUs schedulable, and now sharing one GPU without leaving most of it idle. Chapter 3 picks up what changes once a single GPU genuinely isn't enough, and training has to span more than one.
